Subject: Dedicated fleet sizing: rough numbers + SLOs

Hi Kimberly,

We need Redwood's help sizing dedicated capacity for an upcoming production rollout. High-level details below — happy to do a call but wanted an initial read before budgeting.

- Model: customer will run "rbw-sagebridge-13B-q" (quantized 13B variant)
- Typical request: 512 input tokens + 64 generated tokens (average)
- SLO target: p95 end-to-end < 200ms (apparent from our app UX needs)
- Traffic shape: current beta peaks of ~420 rps (short bursts) and sustained ~180–250 rps for busy hours; we see short concurrent bursts up to ~1,800 active sessions but these are short-lived (tens of seconds)
- Geographical focus: US primary, multi-region later

Questions: can you give a tokens/sec estimate and a baseline committed GPU count to hit p95 <200ms (assume 1.5x headroom for commit)? Also please call out any levers (batching, KV caching, model variants) that materially reduce committed capacity.

I've attached a small sample of our production logs (sagebridge_traffic_sample.csv).

Thanks —

Subject: RE: Dedicated fleet sizing: rough numbers + SLOs

Quick sketch based on the numbers Ethan provided and our verified performance for the 13B quantized family. Notes / assumptions up front:
- Use the conservative model throughput from our runtime: ~4,000 tokens/sec per A100-like GPU when serving short generations with optimized kernels (13B quantized). This assumes continuous batching and warm KV cache.
- Tokens per request = 512 + 64 = 576 tokens (we'll call it 576).
- Peak observed rps (global) = 420 rps -> tokens/sec peak = 420 * 576 = 241,920 t/s
- GPUs required @ peak (no headroom) = 241,920 / 4,000 = 60.48 -> 61 GPUs

Headroom & SLO planning:
- 1.5x headroom (recommended baseline commit) -> 61 * 1.5 = 92 GPUs (round to 92)
- For p95 <200ms we need to budget for tail amplification (JIT cold KV misses, transient queuing). Practically that means reserving additional burst capacity or using prewarmed warm-pools so user-visible p95 stays low.

Levers to reduce committed GPUs:
- Prefix / KV caching for repeated prompts: if you have 30% repeat-rate for prefixes we can effectively reduce tokens traversed on average.
- Model variant: running a 7B-latency-optimized variant for non-critical calls reduces per-request tokens processing and improves p95; we can route lower-risk traffic to that variant.
- Aggressive batching reduces per-token compute overhead but increases tail latency; tradeoff with SLO.

Operational recommendation (first pass):
- Commit: 72 dedicated GPUs (covers base load + warm-pool)
- Burst/autoscale pool: extra 60 GPUs (to absorb peak and cold starts)
- Max autoscale cap: 140 GPUs (safety ceiling)

I'll prototype a more precise spreadsheet with sensitivity buckets (rps / token-size / per-gpu throughput) and share as an attachment.

—Ben

Subject: RE: Dedicated fleet sizing: latency-first runbook + fallback strategy

Adding a latency-first operational plan to Ben's numbers:

High-level: to meet p95 <200ms on quantized 13B we need a combination of reserved warm capacity + dynamic fallback and routing policies. Concrete suggestions:
1) Reserved "fast-slab" (dedicated commit): 72 GPUs located in us-west for lowest RTT to your primary app region. This keeps p95 low for baseline traffic.
2) Warm-pool of 16 GPUs with prewarmed KV cache and pinned sessions to absorb rapid concurrency spikes (short bursts of concurrent sessions). These should be part of the committed slab so warm-state is preserved.
3) Burst/autoscale pool (on-demand) for deeper peaks: 60 GPUs (HPA) using cheaper spot-like instances — route only non-p95-critical traffic here or apply circuit-breaker logic.
4) Model fallback: run a 7B latency-optimized variant behind the same endpoint. If internal queue depth > X or predicted tail > target, shift up to ~30% of traffic to the 7B path. This reduces compute by ~40% on those requests and typically recovers p95.

Capacity math (sensitivity buckets included in attached spreadsheet):
- Baseline sustained rps 250 -> tokens/sec = 250 * 576 = 144,000 t/s -> ~36 GPUs @ 4k t/s
- Peak 420 rps -> 241,920 t/s -> ~61 GPUs @ 4k t/s
- With safety: we recommend commit 72 GPUs to give operational breathing room for KV misses and small model variance.

If they insist on contractual 1.5x headroom baked into commit (to avoid autoscale billing), that maps to ~92 GPUs as Ben noted. Personally I'd recommend committing 72 and buying guaranteed burst bandwidth (or a dedicated burst pool) because it lowers the committed cost while preserving p95 via warm-pool and fallbacks.

Attaching a quick spreadsheet (sagebridge_maths_v1.xlsx) with the sensitivity table and a sample allocation plan.

—Karthik

- Dedicated warm-pool: 16 GPUs prewarmed and pinned for KV cache residency
- Burst pool: up to 60 GPUs autoscale (on-demand) with circuit-breaker routing for non-critical traffic
- Model routing: primary 13B quantized; fallback 7B latency variant for up to 30% of traffic during peaks
- SLA targets: p95 <200ms for traffic routed to the fast-slab; documented fallback behavior for heavy tail periods
- Suggested commercial construct: 12-month commitment for the 72-GPU slab + burst credits for agreed monthly burst minutes (placeholder in MAP).

Next steps:

2) Sign the MAP / DocuSign draft (link in MAP).
